idiom_name: check at the point of use (EAFP) behind a single facade; __getattribute__/descriptors where attribute-level mediation is required
implementation_notes: Python has no enforced privacy - underscore conventions and name mangling only discourage access - so the idiomatic realization is a module-level facade: one public entry per resource that performs the policy check, with __all__ fixing the exported surface. For resources that are checked at the OS level the documented caution is the pattern's own rule: using os.access() to test before opening 'creates a security hole, because the user might exploit the short time interval between checking and opening the file', and the docs point to EAFP instead - attempt the operation and let the mediator own the check - which merges the check and the use into one step. Where attribute access itself must be mediated (a wrapper that must see every read or write), the data model's __getattribute__ and the descriptor protocol are the hooks, and they are documented as bypassable for implicit special-method lookup - mediation for cooperating code, not a security boundary.
pitfalls: Name mangling is not privacy: vault._Vault__store and vars(vault) reach the backing objects, and any caller can replace attributes - the mediator is only as complete as the discipline of the code base.
The documented check-then-open race: os.access() followed by open() is a security hole; use EAFP or a single mediated operation instead.
__getattribute__ is bypassed for implicit special-method lookup and object.__getattribute__ can be called directly, so attribute interception cannot carry the security claim on its own.
Decorator-based checks are bypassed when the undecorated function object is reachable, and caching decorators (lru_cache) hold stale decisions across a revocation.
